summary.text: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist known for formulating the periodic law and creating a version of the periodic table of elements.
He used the law to correct accepted properties of some known elements, such as the valence and atomic weight of uranium.
He also used it to predict the properties of three elements not yet discovered: germanium, gallium and scandium.

paragraphs.heading: The chemist behind the law
paragraphs.text: Dmitri Mendeleev, who lived from 1834 to 1907, was a Russian chemist known for stating the periodic law and building a version of the periodic table. He used that law to correct the accepted values for some known elements, such as uranium's valence and atomic weight. He also used it to forecast the properties of three elements nobody had found yet: germanium, gallium and scandium. The synthetic element mendelevium carries his name.

paragraphs.heading: A Siberian childhood
paragraphs.text: He was born in a village near Tobolsk in Siberia. His father, Ivan, was a school principal and teacher. Dmitri was the youngest of 17 siblings, though sources still disagree on the exact number. When his father went blind and lost his teaching post, his mother went to work and restarted her family's abandoned glass factory. At 13, after his father died and fire destroyed the factory, he attended the Gymnasium in Tobolsk.

paragraphs.heading: Finding a place to study
paragraphs.text: In 1849 his mother took him across Russia to Moscow, hoping to enrol him at the university there, but it turned him away. The two went on to Saint Petersburg, and in 1850 he entered the Main Pedagogical Institute. After graduating he caught tuberculosis and in 1855 moved to the Crimean Peninsula, where he taught science at a gymnasium in Simferopol. He came back to Saint Petersburg in 1857 with his health fully restored.

paragraphs.heading: Rise as a chemist
paragraphs.text: From 1859 to 1861 he worked in Heidelberg on capillarity of liquids and on how the spectroscope works. Later in 1861 he published a textbook, Organic Chemistry, which won him the Demidov Prize. He became a professor at the Saint Petersburg Technological Institute in 1864 and at Saint Petersburg State University in 1865. By 1871 he had turned Saint Petersburg into a chemistry research centre known around the world.

paragraphs.heading: Others saw the pattern too
paragraphs.text: In 1863, 56 elements were known, and roughly one new element was being found each year. Mendeleev was not the first to spot periodicity. John Newlands described a Law of Octaves based on relative atomic weight and published it in 1865; it pointed to possible new elements such as germanium, but the idea was criticized, and the Society of Chemists did not recognize his work until 1887. Lothar Meyer published a paper in 1864 sorting 28 elements by valence, without predicting any new ones.

paragraphs.heading: Patterns in atomic weight
paragraphs.text: Line the elements up by atomic weight and their properties seem to come back again and again in a regular cycle. Elements that are chemically alike either have similar atomic weights, as with Pt, Ir and Os, or have weights that climb in regular steps, as with K, Rb and Cs.
